Kingdom of Priests: A History of Old Testament Israel
A history of Old Testament Israel using the traditional chronology with an Exodus around 1446 BC.
An Egyptologist's survey of the historical evidence for the Old Testament periods, favouring a 13th-century Exodus.

Israel's story runs from a promise made to one man to the coming of one Seed, and through him to every nation. This timeline follows it from Abraham to the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70: the patriarchs, Egypt and Sinai, the judges and kings, division and exile, return and waiting, and then Christ. Three bands under the line show the big picture: the promise came before the nation existed; Israel was God's chosen nation under the old covenant; and through it all the promise was aimed at one Seed, who is Christ.

Dates before about 900 BC are approximate. This timeline follows the traditional chronology built from 1 Kings 6:1 and Exodus 12:40 (an Exodus around 1446 BC); many scholars prefer a later Exodus around 1260 BC, and both are shown where it matters. Christians differ on whether the Jewish people as a nation have a further role in prophecy; this study shows how the New Testament itself reads the promise to Abraham (Galatians 3:16, 29), and the Israel study sets out the other views.
God calls Abram out of Ur and Haran and promises a land, a great nation, and blessing for all the families of the earth through him. The promise comes before there is any nation.
God counts Abram's faith as righteousness, promises offspring as many as the stars, and binds himself alone by walking between the pieces. He foretells 400 years of affliction in a foreign land.
Isaac is born when Abraham is a hundred years old. On Mount Moriah God provides a substitute and repeats the oath: in your offspring all nations will be blessed.
Jacob sees a ladder joining heaven and earth, and later, after wrestling with God, receives the name Israel. Jesus later says he himself is that ladder (John 1:51).
Twelve sons go down to Egypt
Joseph's brothers and Jacob's household, seventy persons, settle in Goshen. Jacob blesses his twelve sons, the heads of the twelve tribes, and promises the sceptre to Judah.
After 430 years in Egypt, God brings Israel out with mighty acts and the Passover lamb. The promise to Abraham was 430 years older than the law (Galatians 3:17).
Mount Sinai: the nation is formed
At Sinai Israel becomes God's covenant nation: a treasured possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation, bound by the law and sealed with blood.
A generation refuses to enter the land and dies in the wilderness; forty years, one for each day the spies were in the land.
Under Joshua Israel crosses the Jordan and takes the land. Not one of God's good promises fails.
A repeating cycle: Israel turns to idols, is oppressed, cries out, and God raises a judge to deliver them. Everyone does what is right in his own eyes.
The people ask for a king like the nations. Saul is anointed, but loses the kingdom through disobedience.
God promises David a son whose throne will be established forever. Peter says God kept this oath by raising Christ to sit on David's throne.
In the 480th year after the Exodus, Solomon begins the temple. Israel reaches its widest borders, from the Euphrates to Egypt.
Rehoboam keeps Judah and Benjamin in the south; Jeroboam leads the ten northern tribes, sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan, and the kingdoms split.
Samaria falls to Assyria and the northern tribes are deported and scattered. Many northerners had already moved south to Judah, and members of the northern tribes appear again in the New Testament.
Nebuchadnezzar takes Daniel and others in 605 BC, more in 597, and in 586 BC burns the temple and Jerusalem. Jeremiah foretells seventy years.
Cyrus allows the exiles to return. A remnant goes back to rebuild, as Isaiah and Jeremiah promised.
The temple is finished under Zerubbabel; Haggai promises that the latter glory of this house will be greater than the former.
Jerusalem's walls are rebuilt “in a troubled time,” and Malachi, the last prophet, promises Elijah before the great day.
In the fullness of time God sends his Son, born in Bethlehem of David's line: the Seed to whom the promise was made.
The cross: the old covenant ends
Jesus dies as the Passover Lamb; the temple curtain is torn. His blood is the new covenant, and the old covenant is made obsolete.
Around twelve Jewish apostles the Spirit forms the new covenant people; three thousand believe, and the gospel goes to Samaria and the nations.
Within a generation, as Jesus warned, Rome destroys Jerusalem and the temple. The old covenant order, ready to vanish, passes away.
Israel does not yet exist as a nation
The promise came first. The law came 430 years after the promise, and could not cancel it (Galatians 3:17).
Israel, the chosen nation under the old covenant
From Sinai to the cross: a kingdom of priests and a holy nation, under the law as a guardian until Christ came (Galatians 3:24).
Forty years: the old order “ready to vanish”
The new covenant began at the cross; the temple and its sacrifices continued until AD 70.
“He saith not, And to seeds, as of many; but as of one, And to thy seed, which is Christ” (Galatians 3:16, KJV)
The promise to Abraham is kept in Christ and in all who belong to him, Jew and Gentile (Galatians 3:29).
After Babel the nations are scattered; God's purpose is still for them all.

How the story arrives at Christ.
When did Israel become a nation?
At Mount Sinai, when God made his covenant with the descendants of Jacob after the Exodus.

Abraham received the promise of a great nation, but for more than four centuries his descendants were a family and then an enslaved people. At Sinai God said that if they kept his covenant they would be his treasured possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. The covenant was sealed with blood (Exodus 24:8). So the promise came first, and the nation was formed later, under the law.
Deuteronomy 26:5: a wandering Aramean was my father … there he became a nation.
Some date Israel's nationhood from the promise to Abraham or from Jacob's renaming.
Why does it matter that the promise came before the nation?
Because the promise rests on faith, not on the law or nationality. Paul argues that the law, given 430 years later, cannot cancel it.

Abraham was counted righteous by faith before he was circumcised and long before the law (Romans 4:9-11). Paul says the law, coming 430 years after the promise, does not annul it. So the promise was always bigger than the nation that carried it: it was for all who share Abraham's faith.
Romans 4:11-12: the father of all who believe.
Dispensationalists agree the promise rests on grace, but hold that its national and land aspects still belong to ethnic Israel.
How are the dates of Abraham and the Exodus worked out?
From the Bible's own numbers: 480 years from the Exodus to Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6:1) and 430 years in Egypt (Exodus 12:40). Many scholars prefer a later Exodus around 1260 BC.

Solomon's temple was begun around 966 BC. Adding 480 years gives an Exodus about 1446 BC; adding 430 years in Egypt and the patriarchs' ages gives Abraham's call around 2091 BC. Archaeologists who favour a 13th-century Exodus point to the city of Rameses (Exodus 1:11). The order of events is the same either way.
Genesis 47:9: Jacob was 130 when he came to Egypt.
Some read the 480 years as twelve generations of forty, a symbolic total.
Because of Solomon's idolatry and Rehoboam's harshness. God tore ten tribes away but kept one tribe for David's sake.

Solomon turned to other gods in his old age, and God told him the kingdom would be torn from his son, except for one tribe for David's sake. When Rehoboam refused to lighten the people's burdens, the northern tribes made Jeroboam king. Jeroboam set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan, and the north never returned to the LORD's temple.
All readings agree on this history.
Were the ten tribes really lost?
Many were deported and absorbed, but people from the northern tribes had already joined Judah, and the New Testament still knows them.

When Jeroboam set up his calves, priests and faithful people from every tribe moved to Judah (2 Chronicles 11:16). Hezekiah invited the north to Passover and some came (2 Chronicles 30:11). Anna the prophetess was of the tribe of Asher (Luke 2:36), and James writes to the twelve tribes (James 1:1). So Israel as a whole was represented in the returning remnant.
Some groups claim descent from the lost tribes; the biblical evidence points to their remnant joining Judah.
Did Israel return from exile as the prophets promised?
Yes. After seventy years Cyrus let the exiles return; they rebuilt the temple and the walls.

Jeremiah promised a return after seventy years. Ezra records Cyrus's decree in 538 BC, the temple finished in 516 BC, and Nehemiah rebuilt the walls in 444 BC. Yet the prophets also promised a greater restoration with a new covenant and the Spirit, which the New Testament says came with Christ.
Some hold that a fuller national return was still to come, beginning in 1948.
What does Paul mean that the promise was to one Seed, Christ?
That the promise to Abraham and his offspring was aimed at one descendant, Christ, and through him belongs to all who are in him.

In Galatians 3:16 Paul points out that God said “and to your seed,” singular, meaning Christ. Then he concludes that all who belong to Christ, Jew or Greek, are Abraham's seed and heirs according to the promise (3:28-29). The story narrows from many nations to one man, to one nation, to one tribe, to one house, to one Seed, and then widens again to every nation.
Genesis 22:18: in your seed all nations will be blessed.
Dispensationalists accept that Christ is the Seed while holding that the physical seed of Abraham still has distinct promises.
Why does the timeline end in AD 70?
Because the destruction of the temple ended the old covenant order that began at Sinai, as Jesus foretold.

The old covenant was made obsolete at the cross (Hebrews 8:13), but the temple and its sacrifices continued for about forty years. Jesus said not one stone would be left on another, within that generation. When Rome destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70, the system that had defined Israel as a nation under the law came to its end. The story continues in the church, the one people of God from every nation.
Hebrews 9:8-10: while the first tent is still standing.
Others continue the timeline to 1948 and expect a future for national Israel in prophecy.
Are the Jewish people still chosen?
Paul says God has not rejected his people, and they remain beloved for the fathers' sake; their salvation comes through Christ, like everyone's.

In Romans 11 Paul insists God has not rejected his people, that a remnant believes, and that the natural branches can be grafted back into their own olive tree. Their election is not cancelled; its goal is Christ. Christians differ on whether a large future turning of Jews to Christ is promised, and on any role for the land.
